full_judgment:
Md Abdur Razzaque J: This Rule arising out of an application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Act V of 1908) at the instance of the petitioner-respondent Santi Bushan Deb is directed against the judgment and order dated 30-4-1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 127 of 1992 reversing the judgment and order dated 9-6-1992 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla in Rent Control Case No. 59 of 1991. 

 2. Short facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner-respondent instituted House Rent Control Case No. 59 of 1991 under section 19(1) of Bari Bhara Niontron Ain, 1992 with the assertion that he was a tenant in respect of the case premises on payment of a monthly rent of Taka 125 to the opposite party appellant bank under a deed of agreement. He then deposited Taka 12000 as an advance in terms of the agreement on condition that Taka 62.50 i.e. 50% will be adjusted as rent from the advance and the balance amount of Taka 6000 will remain as deposit and rent of each month will be paid within 7 days of the next following month. On the basis of that agreement the petitioner paid the rent up to the month of February, 1991 as usual against rent receipts. In spite of that agreement the opposite party bank used to accept the accumulated rents of several months at a time granting rent receipts to the petitioner. The opposite party- appellant bank thereafter suddenly stopped accepting rent on the plea of direction from the higher-authority in spite of offer in time and also gave assurance to the petitioner that after getting instruction from the higher authority rent would be received. On 1-6-1991 the opposite party-appellant bank sent a notice upon the petitioner respondent mentioning that he was a defaulter for non-payment of rent in terms of the agreement and, as such, no rent would be accepted from him. In response to that notice, the petitioner-respondent sent a legal notice on 27-6-1992 along with the rent by money order but the opposite party-appellant bank did not receive the same. Thereafter, the petitioner on 24-7-1991 remitted the rent in lump for an amount of Taka 625 for the months from March to July, 1991 through money order but the said money order came back to the petitioner on 29-7-1991 and thereafter the petitioner deposited the rent with the House Rent Controller. 

 3. The opposite party-appellant bank, on the other hand, by filing a written objection denied the case of the petitioner. However, the specific case of the opposite party-appellant bank is that the petitioner-respondent did not pay rent regularly in terms of the agreement in spite of oral and written demand. Consequently, the opposite party appellant bank had to accept the accumulated rent from him at different times and on 1-6-1991 the petitioner- respondent was informed in writing that no rent would be accepted from him as he was a defaulter and the petitioner was further asked to hand over the vacant possession of the premises to them. Thereafter, in response to that notice, the petitioner-respondent sent a lawyer's notice on 27-6-1991 and rent of 5 months on 24-7-1991, which were refused by the opposite party bank for not being in terms of the agreement. 

 4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge and the House Rent Controller after hearing the parties allowed the House Rent Control Case permitting the petitioner to continue depositing rent before the House Rent Controller. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge and the House Rent Controller, the opposite party-bank preferred the appeal and the learned Subordinate Judge, on hearing the appeal, reversed the judgment and order of the House Rent Controller. Hence the present Rule. 

 5. Mr Abdul Latif, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner-respondent with reference to para 12 of the application, submits that in not considering the mode of receipt of rental in lump by the opposite parties appellant-bank in defiance of the terms of the agreement, the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not considering the fact that in consequence of the notice dated 1-6-1991 issued upon the petitioner-respondent stating him for not being the tenant and to surrender the premises, the latter had to send the rent of 5 months from March 1991 to July, 1991 a bit earlier on 27-6-1991 by him and on its return on 29-7-1991 the latter had to deposit the rents on 5-8-1991 i.e. within time. 

 6. On the other hand, Mr Abdul Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party appellant Bank, contends that the story of receipt of rent in lump would not change the mode of realisation of rental as envisaged in the agreement. He further submits that the transmission of the rents for the months from March to July, 1991 in a lump by Money Order in the prior month of June, i.e. on 27-6-1991 and deposit of rent in lump on 5-8-1991 after return of the rent Money Order on 29-7-1991 are all contrary to the agreement and the law prevailing on the subject and consequently the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in dismissing the Miscellaneous appeal. 

 7. As for myself, I have heard both parties and perused the impugned judgments and orders and other materials on record. Admittedly, the petitioner-respondent was to pay rent of Taka 125 PM after the adjustment of Taka 6000 keeping the balance amount of Taka 6000 as security in terms of the agreement. Further, it appears that as per terms of the agreement, the petitioner-respondent was to pay rent of the premises within 7 days of the next month for which the rent would become due. Now, let us examine the legal position of realisation of rent in lump for 5 months from March to July 1991 or earlier before the month for which the rent had become due and transmission of the same by money order to the landlord in the context of law laid down in section 19(1) of the Bari Bhara Niontron Ain, 1991 (Act No.III of 1991). Relevant provision from the said section is reproduced herein below. 

 Above quoted provisions of law are to be read with section 18 and 18(5) of the Act prescribing the effect of non-realisation of rent as a ground for eviction of a tenant and the mode of realisation of rent. Relevant provisions are laid down as follows: 

 8. From the plain reading of the above quoted provisions of law, it is seen that the responsibility of the tenant in order to protect him from eviction is to pay rent as per the terms of the agreement and, if there be no such agreement, then within 15 days of the next month of the month for which the rent has fallen due. Thus, law provides for realisation of monthly rent by the tenant in two modes only--one within the appointed date in terms of the agreement where exists an agreement and another, while there exists no agreement within 15 days of the next month for which the rent has fallen due but nowhere in the said law regulating the manner of realisation of rent of tenanted premises provides a payment of rents for several months in a lump. Non-receipt of rent within the agreed date or the date fixed by law gives an opportunity to the tenant to have recourse to section 19(1) in order to save him from eviction but he is not authorised to accumulate rent or transmit any rent by money order to the landlord in advance in defiance of the agreement or of law as the case may be. Considering the above position of law, it appears to me that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed no error of law in his decision occasioning failure of justice. Eventually, I find no substance in the Rule. The impugned judgment and order of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge are affirmed. The order of stay granted by this Court stands vacated.
